claim: Kirrel3 protein is enriched in synaptosomes prepared from hippocampal lysates with greatest enrichment at postnatal day (P) 21.
source: Kirrel3 protein is enriched in synaptosomes prepared from hippocampal lysates with greatest enrichment at postnatal day (P) 21 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A comparing synaptosome fractions at different developmental timepoints.

claim: In hippocampal neurons cultured for 14 days in vitro (DIV), Kirrel3 localizes to puncta adjacent to the pre- and post-synaptic markers vGlut1 and MAGUK in wild-type but not knockout neurons.
source: In hippocampal neurons cultured for 14 days in vitro (DIV), Kirrel3 localizes to puncta adjacent to the pre- and post-synaptic markers vGlut1 and MAGUK in wild-type but not knockout neurons (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B,C comparing wild-type and knockout neurons.

claim: Kirrel3 localizes to perisynaptic adhesion zones rather than the synaptic cleft.
source: This suggests that, like cadherins, Kirrel3 localizes to perisynaptic adhesion zones rather than the synaptic cleft.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Kirrel3 is adjacent to, not overlapping with, synaptic markers, and compared to known cadherin localization.

claim: Surface FLAG-Kirrel3 is seen as puncta on axons and dendrites of 14DIV neurons.
source: Surface FLAG-Kirrel3 is seen as puncta on axons and dendrites of 14DIV neurons (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by live labeling immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: Prior to synaptogenesis in 4DIV neurons, FLAG-Kirrel3 has a punctate distribution in axons and dendrites and clusters at axon–dendrite contact points.
source: Moreover, even prior to synaptogenesis in 4DIV neurons, FLAG-Kirrel3 already has a punctate distribution in axons and dendrites and clusters at axon–dendrite contact points (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by live labeling immunostaining data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Neither nephrin nor the other Kirrel family members, Kirrel1 and Kirrel2, have appreciable expression in the hippocampus.
source: However, neither nephrin nor the other Kirrel family members, Kirrel1 and Kirrel2, have appreciable expression in the hippocampus (Putaala et al., 2001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

claim: Kirrel3 clusters at cell junctions.
source: We noticed Kirrel3 clusters at cell junctions (Figure 1I,J)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in 293HEK cells shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: Kirrel3 mediates trans-cellular homophilic binding.
source: We demonstrate Kirrel3 mediates trans-cellular homophilic binding (Figure 1K–M and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by cell aggregation assay data shown in Figure 1K-M and Fc binding assay in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Kirrel3 is present at early axon–dendrite contacts.
source: Taken together, our data indicate Kirrel3 is present at early axon–dendrite contacts, localizes at or near synapses, and is a bona fide homophilic adhesion molecule, all of which implicate Kirrel3 in synapse development.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental observations including early punctate distribution and clustering at axon-dendrite contacts.

claim: Kirrel3 is a bona fide homophilic adhesion molecule.
source: Taken together, our data indicate Kirrel3 is present at early axon–dendrite contacts, localizes at or near synapses, and is a bona fide homophilic adhesion molecule, all of which implicate Kirrel3 in synapse development.
evidence: Supported by cell aggregation and Fc binding assays demonstrating homophilic interactions.

claim: In developing P14 and adult hippocampi, Kirrel3 mRNA is present in two cell types: (1) DG neurons and (2) scattered cells of the hilus and area CA3.
source: In developing P14 and adult hippocampi, Kirrel3 mRNA is present in two cell types: (1) DG neurons and (2) scattered cells of the hilus and area CA3 (Figure 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Kirrel3 protein is present in the molecular and stratum lucidum layers of the hippocampus, containing DG dendrites and axons, respectively.
source: Correspondingly, Kirrel3 protein is present in the molecular and stratum lucidum layers of the hippocampus, containing DG dendrites and axons, respectively (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Kirrel3 protein is present in scattered cells of the hilus and area CA3.
source: It is also present in scattered cells of the hilus and area CA3 (Figure 2F)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Kirrel3 protein is faintly present in the stratum lacunosum-moleculare, which contains axons from entorhinal cortex.
source: and faintly in the stratum lacunosum-moleculare, which contains axons from entorhinal cortex.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining experiments, indicating Kirrel3 expression in entorhinal cortex axons.

claim: No Kirrel3 signal was detected in knockout mice.
source: No Kirrel3 signal was detected in knockout mice (Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Kirrel3 knockout mice express membrane-associated GFP instead of Kirrel3.
source: Instead, Kirrel3 knockout mice have farnesylated GFP in frame after exon 1 so they express membrane-associated GFP instead of Kirrel3 (Prince et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prince et al., 2013 describing the knockout mouse generation.

claim: Kirrel3 is selectively expressed by DG neurons and scattered cells of area CA3.
source: Examination of GFP expression in knockout mice indicates that again, Kirrel3 is selectively expressed by DG neurons and scattered cells of area CA3 (Figure 2I–O).
evidence: Supported by GFP immunostaining in knockout mice shown in Figure 2I-O.

claim: Kirrel3 is not expressed at detectable levels in CA3 neurons.
source: Notably, we never observe GFP expression in CA3 neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by GFP immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Nearly all Kirrel3-expressing cells express GABA.
source: We find that nearly all Kirrel3-expressing cells express GABA (Figure 2S).
evidence: Supported by co-immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 2S.

claim: About 20% of all GABA neurons in area CA3 express Kirrel3.
source: Conversely, about 20% of all GABA neurons in area CA3 express Kirrel3 (Figure 2S).
evidence: Supported by co-immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 2S.

claim: Two thirds (about 67%) of Kirrel3/GABA neurons express calbindin.
source: We also co-stained with several common GABA neuron markers and find that two thirds (about 67%) of Kirrel3/GABA neurons express calbindin (Figure 2P–S)
evidence: Supported by co-immunostaining quantification shown in Figure 2P-S.

claim: Kirrel3-positive neurons make up about half of all calbindin-positive interneurons.
source: and these Kirrel3-positive neurons make up about half of all calbindin-positive interneurons.
evidence: Inferred from the quantification data showing overlap between Kirrel3 and calbindin expression.

claim: Glutamatergic DG neurons highly express Kirrel3 and calbindin.
source: Notably, glutamatergic DG neurons also highly express Kirrel3 and calbindin, providing a shared molecular profile between these neuronal populations.
evidence: Observed from immunostaining data showing both DG neurons and certain GABA neurons express Kirrel3 and calbindin.

claim: Complete loss of Kirrel3 does not change cell fate or induce cell death of the neurons examined.
source: Kirrel3 cell populations are similar in P14 Kirrel3 heterozygous and knockout mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), suggesting that complete loss of Kirrel3 does not change cell fate or induce cell death of the neurons examined.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of cell populations between heterozygous and knockout mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the hippocampus, DG neurons and a subset of calbindin-positive GABA neurons selectively express Kirrel3.
source: Taken together, we find that, in the hippocampus, DG neurons and a subset of calbindin-positive GABA neurons selectively express Kirrel3.
evidence: Summarizes multiple immunostaining and quantification experiments.

claim: Kirrel3 knockout mice have significantly fewer and shorter filopodia than wild-type at P14.
source: We discovered Kirrel3 knockout mice have significantly fewer and shorter filopodia than wild-type (Figure 3B–M and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by DiI labeling and morphological quantification shown in Figure 3B-M and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The main bouton area and perimeter are not affected by loss of Kirrel3 at P14.
source: In contrast, the main bouton area and perimeter are not affected by loss of Kirrel3 (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: Supported by morphological quantification shown in Figure 3J,K.

claim: TE spine head density and length are similar between P21 Kirrel3 wild-type and knockout mice.
source: TE spine head density and length are similar between P21 Kirrel3 wild-type and knockout mice (Figure 3P,Q).
evidence: Supported by CA3 neuron spine analysis shown in Figure 3P,Q.

claim: Kirrel3 knockout mice have significant morphological defects in MF filopodia but not in pre- or post-synaptic structures of main MF synapses.
source: Thus, Kirrel3 knockout mice have significant morphological defects in MF filopodia but not in pre- or post-synaptic structures of main MF synapses, suggesting that the number of DG synapses onto GABA neurons is reduced in Kirrel3 knockout mice.
evidence: Inferred from the selective reduction in filopodia without changes in main bouton or TE spine morphology.

claim: The number of DG synapses onto GABA neurons is reduced in Kirrel3 knockout mice.
source: Thus, Kirrel3 knockout mice have significant morphological defects in MF filopodia but not in pre- or post-synaptic structures of main MF synapses, suggesting that the number of DG synapses onto GABA neurons is reduced in Kirrel3 knockout mice.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in MF filopodia, which are the structures that synapse with GABA neurons.

claim: P14–P16 Kirrel3 knockout mice have a significantly increased excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) ratio compared to wild-type mice.
source: As predicted by our model, P14–P16 Kirrel3 knockout mice have a significantly increased excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) ratio compared to wild-type mice (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Evoked responses were due to MF stimulation as confirmed by DCG-IV application.
source: We confirmed evoked responses were due to MF stimulation by applying DCG-IV, a metabotropic glutamate receptor agonist that selectively inhibits MF release (Figure 4A) (Kamiya et al., 1996; Yoshino et al., 1996; Torborg et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings with DCG-IV shown in Figure 4A and cited literature.

claim: With stimulation, P14 knockout mice have a twofold increase in cFos-positive CA3 neurons compared to wild-type.
source: At this age, basal, unstimulated cFos expression is low regardless of genotype, but with stimulation, P14 knockout mice have a twofold increase in cFos-positive CA3 neurons compared to wild-type (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by cFos immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Exploration was comparable between genotypes during cFos stimulation experiments.
source: As a control, mice were recorded and exploration was comparable between genotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral tracking data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: At P14 the CA3 is dominated by inhibition.
source: Interestingly, the number of cFos-positive neurons did not significantly increase in wild-type mice after stimulation but this is consistent with previous reports (Waters et al., 1997) and likely reflects that at P14 the CA3 is dominated by inhibition (Figure 4B, note wild-type E/I ratio is <1) (Torborg et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by E/I ratio data in Figure 4B and cited literature.

claim: No significant differences between wild-type and Kirrel3 knockout neurons in mEPSC amplitude or frequency were found for CA3 or DG neurons.
source: No significant differences between wild-type and Kirrel3 knockout neurons in mEPSC amplitude or frequency were found for either cell type (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Kirrel3 selectively regulates formation of filopodial DG-GABA MF synapses.
source: Together, our functional data support the hypothesis that Kirrel3 selectively regulates formation of filopodial DG-GABA MF synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of morphological and functional data showing selective effects on filopodia and E/I ratio.

claim: Both genotypes have fewer filopodia as adults than at P14.
source: Both genotypes have fewer filopodia as adults than at P14 (compare Figure 4E and Figure 3H), suggesting age-dependent filopodia refinement is Kirrel3-independent.
evidence: Supported by comparison of morphological data between P14 (Figure 3H) and adult (Figure 4E).

claim: Age-dependent filopodia refinement is Kirrel3-independent.
source: Both genotypes have fewer filopodia as adults than at P14 (compare Figure 4E and Figure 3H), suggesting age-dependent filopodia refinement is Kirrel3-independent.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both wild-type and knockout mice show similar developmental reduction in filopodia number.

claim: Adult knockout mice have fewer filopodia and a smaller main bouton.
source: However, while P14 knockout mice have fewer filopodia with a normal main bouton, adult knockout mice have fewer filopodia and a smaller main bouton (Figure 4E–J).
evidence: Supported by morphological quantification shown in Figure 4E-J.

claim: MF synapse defects worsen with age in Kirrel3 knockout mice.
source: Thus, MF synapse defects worsen with age in Kirrel3 knockout mice.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of P14 and adult morphological data showing additional defects in adult mice.

claim: Unstimulated and stimulated cFos expression in CA3 neurons is similar between P60 adult wild-type and knockout mice.
source: In support, unstimulated and stimulated cFos expression in CA3 neurons is similar between P60 adult wild-type and knockout mice (Figure 4K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by cFos immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 4K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A reduction in MF filopodia during development leads to hyper-activation of CA3 neurons that, with time, causes homeostatic mechanisms to decrease the size of the main DG-CA3 MF synapse and return overall CA3 activity levels to a set point.
source: Thus, our data suggest a model in which a reduction in MF filopodia during development leads to hyper-activation of CA3 neurons that, with time, causes homeostatic mechanisms to decrease the size of the main DG-CA3 MF synapse and return overall CA3 activity levels to a set point.
evidence: Speculative model proposed to explain the developmental progression of phenotypes observed in knockout mice.

claim: Adult Kirrel3 knockout mice have only mild hyperactivity and a moderate impairment in novel object recognition compared to wild-type.
source: Kirrel3 knockout mice have only mild hyperactivity and a moderate impairment in novel object recognition compared to wild-type (Choi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2015 describing behavioral tests.

claim: CA3 neuron activity is significantly impaired in 14-day-old animals but returns to normal by 2 months of age.
source: Our results indicate CA3 neuron activity is significantly impaired in 14-day-old animals but returns to normal by 2 months of age.
evidence: Supported by cFos expression data at P14 and P60.

claim: Adult Kirrel3 knockout mice have only moderate behavioral impairments because CA3 neuron activity returns to normal by 2 months of age.
source: This may explain why adult Kirrel3 knockout mice have only moderate behavioral impairments and suggests that younger animals may have more severe behavioral problems.
evidence: Speculative explanation connecting the normalization of CA3 activity in adults to the mild behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Younger animals may have more severe behavioral problems than adult Kirrel3 knockout mice.
source: This may explain why adult Kirrel3 knockout mice have only moderate behavioral impairments and suggests that younger animals may have more severe behavioral problems.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on the observation of more severe CA3 activity defects in young animals.

claim: Kirrel3 is required for normal development of MF filopodia, the synaptic structures connecting DG and GABA neurons.
source: In summary, we demonstrate Kirrel3 is required for normal development of MF filopodia, the synaptic structures connecting DG and GABA neurons.
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis showing reduced filopodia in knockout mice.

claim: Trans-cellular Kirrel3 interactions may stabilize MF filopodia contact and subsequent synapse formation between Kirrel3-expressing cells.
source: Because Kirrel3 is a homophilic adhesion molecule expressed by DG neurons and calbindin-positive GABA neurons in hippocampal area CA3, our work suggests trans-cellular Kirrel3 interactions may stabilize MF filopodia contact and subsequent synapse formation between Kirrel3-expressing cells.
evidence: Speculative mechanism proposed based on Kirrel3's homophilic binding properties and expression pattern.

claim: Kirrel3 is required to maintain feed-forward inhibition and constrain CA3 neuron activity in young animals.
source: Functionally, we demonstrate Kirrel3 is required to maintain feed-forward inhibition and constrain CA3 neuron activity in young animals.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological and cFos data showing increased E/I ratio and CA3 activity in young knockout mice.

claim: Kirrel3 is among the first molecules shown to selectively act on MF filopodia.
source: Although a few molecules have been shown to generally affect MF presynapse formation (Danzer et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2011; Lanore et al., 2012; Wilke et al., 2012), Kirrel3 is among the first shown to selectively act on MF filopodia and our results provide evidence that main and filopodial MF synapse formation can be uncoupled.
evidence: Supported by comparison to cited literature and the selective morphological defects observed in knockout mice.

claim: Main and filopodial MF synapse formation can be uncoupled.
source: Although a few molecules have been shown to generally affect MF presynapse formation (Danzer et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2011; Lanore et al., 2012; Wilke et al., 2012), Kirrel3 is among the first shown to selectively act on MF filopodia and our results provide evidence that main and filopodial MF synapse formation can be uncoupled.
evidence: Supported by the observation that filopodia are affected while main boutons are initially normal in knockout mice.

claim: Calbindin-positive GABA neurons may receive a substantial fraction of DG MF input and be a critical component of feed-forward inhibitory circuits regulating CA3 activity.
source: The role of calbindin-positive GABA neurons in the hippocampus is little studied, but our findings suggest they may receive a substantial fraction of DG MF input and be a critical component of feed-forward inhibitory circuits regulating CA3 activity.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the expression pattern of Kirrel3 and the functional consequences of its loss.

claim: Alterations in the Kirrel3 gene are associated with autism and intellectual disabilities.
source: Given that alterations in the Kirrel3 gene are associated with autism and intellectual disabilities, this work provides the first insight into cellular mechanisms that may underlie Kirrel3-dependent neurological disorders.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge from human genetic studies.

claim: This work provides the first insight into cellular mechanisms that may underlie Kirrel3-dependent neurological disorders.
source: Given that alterations in the Kirrel3 gene are associated with autism and intellectual disabilities, this work provides the first insight into cellular mechanisms that may underlie Kirrel3-dependent neurological disorders.
evidence: Claim about the novelty and significance of the current study's findings.

claim: Kirrel3 loss selectively reduces excitatory synapses made onto inhibitory neurons in hippocampal area CA3.
source: Our work suggests Kirrel3 loss selectively reduces excitatory synapses made onto inhibitory neurons in hippocampal area CA3.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in MF filopodia that synapse with GABA neurons.

claim: CA3 neurons are over-active in young Kirrel3 knockout animals.
source: Consequently, CA3 neurons are over-active in young Kirrel3 knockout animals.
evidence: Supported by increased E/I ratio and cFos expression in young knockout mice.

claim: Altered E/I ratios are hypothesized to underlie neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Altered E/I ratios are hypothesized to underlie neurodevelopmental disorders (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Baroncelli et al., 2011; Fakhoury, 2015), and our work suggests this may be an important circuit defect of Kirrel3-associated diseases.
evidence: Supported by cited literature proposing E/I imbalance as a mechanism in neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim: Altered E/I ratio may be an important circuit defect of Kirrel3-associated diseases.
source: Altered E/I ratios are hypothesized to underlie neurodevelopmental disorders (Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Baroncelli et al., 2011; Fakhoury, 2015), and our work suggests this may be an important circuit defect of Kirrel3-associated diseases.
evidence: Speculative connection between the observed E/I imbalance in knockout mice and human Kirrel3-associated disorders.

claim: Such a strong imbalance probably would not occur if all synapses were equally impaired.
source: Interestingly, such a strong imbalance probably would not occur if all synapses were equally impaired.
evidence: Logical inference about the importance of synaptic specificity in circuit function.

claim: Loss of synaptic specificity molecules can cause widespread circuit dysfunction.
source: In this way, loss of synaptic specificity molecules can cause widespread circuit dysfunction.
evidence: General principle inferred from the specific findings about Kirrel3.

claim: There is much evidence that hippocampal circuits are altered in autism and intellectual disabilities.
source: There is much evidence that hippocampal circuits are altered in autism and intellectual disabilities, but it is likely not the only brain region affected in these complex neurological disorders (Philip et al., 2012; Zoghbi and Bear, 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature on autism and intellectual disabilities.

claim: The hippocampus is likely not the only brain region affected in autism and intellectual disabilities.
source: There is much evidence that hippocampal circuits are altered in autism and intellectual disabilities, but it is likely not the only brain region affected in these complex neurological disorders (Philip et al., 2012; Zoghbi and Bear, 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited literature and general knowledge about neurodevelopmental disorders.

claim: Kirrel3 is expressed by specific populations of neurons outside the hippocampus.
source: Kirrel3 is also expressed by specific populations of neurons outside the hippocampus (Lein et al., 2007; Choi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited literature describing Kirrel3 expression patterns.

claim: Kirrel3 may regulate formation of other specific types of synapses throughout the brain.
source: Thus, Kirrel3 may also regulate formation of other specific types of synapses throughout the brain, which may further contribute to its association with neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation from hippocampal findings to other brain regions.

claim: Copy number variations and exonic point mutations in the Kirrel3 gene are associated with intellectual disability, autism, and Jacobsen's syndrome.
source: In humans, copy number variations and exonic point mutations in the Kirrel3 gene are associated with intellectual disability, autism, and Jacobsen's syndrome, a rare developmental disorder that often includes intellectual disabilities (Bhalla et al., 2008; Guerin et al., 2012; Michaelson et al., 2012; Neale et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited human genetic studies.

claim: The Kirrel ortholog SYG-1 regulates synapse formation and axon branching in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: The Kirrel ortholog SYG-1 regulates synapse formation and axon branching in Caenorhabditis elegans (Shen and Bargmann, 2003; Chia et al., 2014), but the role of Kirrel3 in mammalian synapse development is unknown.
evidence: Supported by cited literature on C. elegans SYG-1.

claim: Kirrel3 is a target-specific cue at MF synapses.
source: Here, we demonstrate Kirrel3 is a target-specific cue at MF synapses.
evidence: Supported by the selective effects on DG-GABA synapses but not DG-CA3 synapses.

claim: Kirrel3 specifically regulates development of DG-GABA MF filopodia, which are necessary to constrain excitatory drive to CA3 neurons after DG stimulation.
source: Kirrel3 specifically regulates development of DG-GABA MF filopodia, which are necessary to constrain excitatory drive to CA3 neurons after DG stimulation.
evidence: Supported by morphological and functional data showing reduced filopodia and increased CA3 activity in knockout mice.

claim: Subtle synaptic changes during development impact circuit function.
source: Our findings demonstrate that subtle synaptic changes during development impact circuit function and provide the first insight toward understanding the cellular basis of Kirrel3-dependent neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: General conclusion drawn from the specific findings about Kirrel3's effects on synapses and circuits.

claim: The main DG-CA3 synapse consists of a giant presynaptic bouton apposed to a multi-headed CA3 spine called a thorny excrescence (TE).
source: The main DG-CA3 synapse consists of a giant presynaptic bouton apposed to a multi-headed CA3 spine called a thorny excrescence (TE).
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about mossy fiber synapses.

claim: Filopodia project from the main bouton and synapse with nearby GABA neurons.
source: In addition, filopodia project from the main bouton and synapse with nearby GABA neurons (Frotscher, 1989; Acsády et al., 1998).
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge supported by cited literature.

claim: Filopodial MF synapses mediate feed-forward inhibition of CA3 neurons and are essential for hippocampal function during learning and memory tasks.
source: Filopodial MF synapses mediate feed-forward inhibition of CA3 neurons and are essential for hippocampal function during learning and memory tasks (Torborg et al., 2010; Ruediger et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by cited literature on the function of filopodial MF synapses.

claim: Main bouton and filopodial MF synapses have different molecular and functional properties.
source: Although main bouton and filopodial MF synapses are physically linked, they have different molecular and functional properties (Toth et al., 2000; McBain, 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited literature describing differences between the two synapse types.

claim: DG neurons utilize specific cues to construct different types of synapses with CA3 and GABA neurons.
source: This suggests DG neurons utilize specific cues to construct different types of synapses with CA3 and GABA neurons, but the identity of the target-specific cues is unknown.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that physically linked synapses have different properties.

claim: Kirrels have been studied during formation of the kidney slit diaphragm in mice.
source: In mice, Kirrels have been studied during formation of the kidney slit diaphragm, an adhesive cell junction for filtering blood (Donoviel et al., 2001; George and Holzman, 2012)
evidence: Supported by cited literature on Kirrel function in kidney.

claim: Kirrels have been studied in axon targeting of the olfactory and vomeronasal systems in mice.
source: and in axon targeting of the olfactory and vomeronasal systems (Serizawa et al., 2006; Prince et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by cited literature on Kirrel function in sensory systems.

claim: Synaptic target specificity is critical for brain function.
source: Synaptic target specificity, whereby neurons make distinct types of synapses with different target cells, is critical for brain function, yet the mechanisms driving it are poorly understood.
evidence: General principle based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: The mechanisms driving synaptic target specificity are poorly understood.
source: Synaptic target specificity, whereby neurons make distinct types of synapses with different target cells, is critical for brain function, yet the mechanisms driving it are poorly understood.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Loss of Kirrel3 robustly increases CA3 neuron activity in developing mice.
source: Consequently, loss of Kirrel3 robustly increases CA3 neuron activity in developing mice.
evidence: Supported by E/I ratio and cFos data in young knockout mice.

claim: Kirrel3 is required for formation of MF filopodia.
source: Here, we show Kirrel3 is required for formation of MF filopodia; the structures that give rise to DG-GABA synapses and that regulate feed-forward inhibition of CA3 neurons.
evidence: Supported by morphological analysis showing reduced filopodia in knockout mice.

claim: MF filopodia give rise to DG-GABA synapses.
source: Here, we show Kirrel3 is required for formation of MF filopodia; the structures that give rise to DG-GABA synapses and that regulate feed-forward inhibition of CA3 neurons.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about mossy fiber structure.

claim: MF filopodia regulate feed-forward inhibition of CA3 neurons.
source: Here, we show Kirrel3 is required for formation of MF filopodia; the structures that give rise to DG-GABA synapses and that regulate feed-forward inhibition of CA3 neurons.
evidence: Established functional knowledge supported by the current study's findings.

claim: The role of Kirrel3 at synapses remained largely unknown prior to this study.
source: Alterations in the Kirrel3 gene are repeatedly associated with intellectual disabilities, but the role of Kirrel3 at synapses remained largely unknown.
evidence: Statement about the gap in knowledge that this study addresses.
